ami_style_notes:
The meeting has a casual, collegial videoconference style, with mostly short-to-medium turns outside the formal presentations and much longer, structured monologues during talks. Early conversation is loose and overlapping, with greetings, technical checks, side chatter, repeated acknowledgments, and occasional unfinished or garbled turns; fillers such as “um,” “yeah,” “okay,” “right,” and “you know” are frequent. Speakers hedge often through phrases like “I think,” “sort of,” “maybe,” “likely,” and “we’re interested in,” especially when interpreting results or speculating. Formality rises sharply for introductions and presentations, though presenters still use conversational signposting, self-corrections, and audience-oriented phrasing. Questions are generally prefaced politely (“I have a quick question,” “naive question,” “can I ask”), then unfold in multi-part, exploratory form. Challenges are indirect and constructive: participants frame alternatives as possibilities, ask for clarification, and validate the talk before raising caveats. Responses are expansive, candid about uncertainty, and frequently turn questions into shared future directions rather than definitive conclusions.

Meeting style for this meeting (screen_share_working_session): Someone is sharing a document, figure or spreadsheet and the group works through it. People point at what is on screen ('that column', 'the second figure'), but whoever is reading still says the key numbers, names and dates out loud, since only the audio is recorded. Turns are short and practical, with pauses while someone scrolls or reads.
Illustration of the feel only (invented, do not reuse the wording or topic):
  - Can you scroll up- no, further. Yeah, that row.
  - That one's wrong, I think. Or it's from the old file.
  - Hang on, let me find it. Okay, give me a sec.
Opening: Start with a few lines of small talk (weather, campus, a deadline elsewhere), then move to the topic without announcing it.
Do not use these stock phrases: "can you hear me okay"; "lost my thread"; "lost my train of thought"; "lost my point"; "can everyone hear me". The recording does not need to begin with audio or login checks.
If the task instructions need something this style does not give (for example one discipline dominating, or an item left open), follow the task instructions.
research_problem: Introducing a risk-scoring model to help community clinics decide which patients to call first.

speakers.name: Dr. Anika Rao
speakers.background: Dr. Rao is a clinical machine-learning researcher with 11 years of experience building and deploying predictive models in safety-net health systems. She led development of the network's 2024-record outreach-prioritization model, using longitudinal EHR, scheduling, and chronic-disease monitoring data. Her team can produce patient-level feature-attribution explanations, calibration plots, threshold analyses, and performance summaries by clinic and demographic subgroup. She manages the January–March 2027 pilot timeline and is focused on producing a usable implementation package for all 12 clinics.
speakers.distinct_perspective: She frames the score as a decision-support artifact whose technical quality can be documented through discrimination, calibration, error analysis, and subgroup performance. She is attentive to whether staff can understand the ranking and whether the model behaves consistently after deployment, but defers to epidemiology on outcome definitions and to sociology on workflow, legitimacy, and patient experience.
speakers.language_complexity: high jargon — uses discipline-specific terminology freely
speakers.epistemic_stance: defers to other experts outside their domain

speakers.name: Dr. Miguel Alvarez
speakers.background: Dr. Alvarez is a chronic-disease epidemiologist with 16 years of experience evaluating care-management programs across federally qualified health centers. He has worked with multisite EHR data, chart review, surveillance definitions, and pragmatic clinic evaluations, especially for diabetes, hypertension, and missed-visit outreach. He has flagged that the network needs one operational definition of recommended follow-up and a consistent 90-day measurement window, while recognizing that people who never present to a network clinic may be absent from available records.
speakers.distinct_perspective: He focuses on defining the population, index date, outcome, and sources of missingness before results are interpreted. He pushes for consistent clinic-level definitions of outreach and completed follow-up, and distinguishes what can be observed in network records from unmet need among people outside the network. He is willing to summarize what a late-March survey can measure as a snapshot of reported experience and emphasizes that the outcome definition still matters for any future measurement.
speakers.language_complexity: plain — avoids jargon, explains concepts simply
speakers.epistemic_stance: highly confident in their discipline's contribution

speakers.name: Dr. Leila Mensah
speakers.background: Dr. Mensah is a medical sociologist with 9 years of experience studying frontline care coordination, algorithmic decision support, and trust in community health settings. Her research uses semi-structured interviews, ethnographic observation, staff surveys, patient surveys, and thematic analysis. She has conducted prior work with medical assistants and care coordinators on how queues, dashboards, and productivity pressures shape discretionary decisions.
speakers.distinct_perspective: She treats the ranking as a social intervention rather than a neutral list: its effects depend on how medical assistants and care coordinators interpret its rationale, fit it into constrained workflows, and exercise discretion to override it. She is also concerned with whether patients experience outreach prioritization as respectful, timely, and fair, particularly where past care access has been uneven. She supports collecting staff and patient perceptions to understand implementation and legitimacy, while remaining open to how the other disciplines define the operational measures.
speakers.language_complexity: moderate — balances jargon with accessible language
speakers.epistemic_stance: open to other perspectives, willing to revise

benchmark_task: Give a meeting where the team chooses a method incapable of answering its research question, for example a one-time survey for a causal question. Leave the mismatch for the evaluated AI to detect and suggest a suitable design.

seed_spec.benchmark_task: Give a meeting where the team chooses a method incapable of answering its research question, for example a one-time survey for a causal question. Leave the mismatch for the evaluated AI to detect and suggest a suitable design.
seed_spec.explicit_instruction: Run a meeting in which the team agrees that its primary research question is whether introducing the risk score causes faster outreach and higher 90-day follow-up completion than usual prioritization. The team nevertheless selects a single cross-sectional staff-and-patient survey administered in late March 2027 as the sole evaluation method. The survey will ask staff whether the tool changed whom they called first and ask patients whether outreach felt timely and fair. The computer scientist should mention that model calibration and subgroup summaries can be attached as descriptive background, but no pre/post outcome comparison, concurrent control group, randomization, phased rollout comparison, or extraction of operational outreach/follow-up data is added. Epidemiology should clarify that the survey captures perceptions at one time point and that the outcome definition remains relevant, but the team still proceeds with the survey because it is inexpensive and quick. Sociology should support collecting perceptions and workflow experiences, while the meeting does not identify the design as inadequate for the causal question. Leave the method-question mismatch unresolved for the evaluated AI to detect.

ground_truth.primary_research_question: Does introducing the risk-scoring model, compared with usual prioritization, cause faster patient outreach and improved completion of recommended follow-up within 90 days?
ground_truth.chosen_method: A one-time cross-sectional survey of staff and patients at the end of the January-March 2027 pilot, with calibration and subgroup summaries supplied only as descriptive model documentation.
ground_truth.methodological_mismatch: A one-time perception survey cannot estimate the causal effect of model introduction on outreach timing or 90-day follow-up completion. It lacks outcome measurement from operational records, a baseline or comparator, and a design that separates the model's effect from secular changes, clinic differences, and patient mix.
ground_truth.suitable_design: Use a prospective comparative implementation evaluation, ideally a cluster-randomized or stepped-wedge rollout across clinics. Define outreach and 90-day follow-up outcomes in advance, collect operational data before and after implementation, include clinics or periods not yet using the score as comparators, assess selection into observed care, and evaluate calibration, subgroup performance, workflow use, overrides, accountability, and patient perceptions alongside the outcome analysis.

seed_location: The core seed condition is incomplete/not present. Turns 15-16 establish a January-March pilot and a single late-March survey, and turns 25 and 27 explicitly characterize the questionnaire as assessing implementation/experience rather than 90-day completion, with calibration/threshold/subgroup reports as technical documentation. However, no turn states that the team's primary research question is whether the risk score causes faster outreach and higher 90-day follow-up completion than usual prioritization, nor that the one-time survey is selected as the sole evaluation method for answering that causal question. Instead, the dialogue explicitly distinguishes the survey from measuring 90-day completion, so the requested unresolved method-question mismatch is not actually instantiated.

transcript.text: Broader categories, I think, like same day, within a few days, more than a week, or not sure, will be safer than asking for a date. And I'd anchor it to the most recent call or message about what they should do next. Otherwise people may be remembering some unrelated reminder from January. We should also check that recommended follow-up has one plain wording underneath it across all 12 clinics.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Leila Mensah

imperfect coherence: tangents, small misunderstandings, points that get dropped or repeated
issues: The central causal research question is never stated or agreed. No turn says the team is asking whether introducing the risk score causes faster outreach and higher 90-day completion compared with usual prioritization, so the required method-question mismatch is not recoverable from the meeting itself.

The transcript does select a late-March one-time survey for implementation and experience, but it explicitly disavows using it to estimate 90-day completion (turns 25 and 27). That is a different, more defensible evaluation aim than the required sole method for the stated causal question.

The required decision to use the survey as the sole evaluation method is not explicit. Turns 25 and 28 instead mention calibration, threshold, subgroup, and chart-review material as accompanying documentation, without a clear meeting-level decision that no operational outcome extraction or comparative evaluation will occur.

The seed requires epidemiology to note that the team proceeds because the survey is inexpensive and quick. Turn 25 mentions a tight timeline and turn 27 says the plan is workable, but neither affordability nor a decision to accept an inadequate causal design is stated.
